assets.title: The Doors
assets.summary: Look at the door (or doors) the Fade came in through — and sharpen them.

steps.title: How the gap opened
steps.prompt: When we first talked, you told me how the gap opened. Does that still feel right — or is there more to it now?
steps.companion_frame: You already gave this a name once, when we first met. You know yourself better a few steps in, so let's look at it together — keep what fits, sharpen the wording, and we can add one if another's been quietly in the room.
steps.probe: The Door is the category; what it actually was for you is the part that matters. Tell me your version.

steps.title: More than one
steps.prompt: Did more than one door open around the same time? If another fits, tell me.
steps.companion_frame: Most people walked through more than one — the body starts saying no AND the role ends; the house quiets AND a parent gets sick. There's no prize for keeping it simple; the fuller picture is what lets me meet you where you actually are.
steps.probe: Even if it feels smaller — which other one's been in the room?

steps.title: Saying it back
steps.prompt: Say it back in a sentence: 'The Fade came in through ___.'
steps.companion_frame: A lot of good people have walked through these — and most never had a word for it. Putting a word to the Door doesn't fix it; it just means you stop pretending it isn't there.
steps.probe: Own it as yours — not only a thing that happened to you, but a door you walked through and can walk back out of.

close.companion: Your Doors are sharpened and current now, up on your dashboard. You can't close a door you won't look at. I've put what surfaced in your Playbook to keep or cut.
close.prompt: Ready to dig for what's underneath?

assets.title: The Drift Quiz
assets.summary: An honest read of what the Fade cost, and how far you've drifted.

steps.title: Be honest what it cost
steps.prompt: Name three things the Fade cost you — be specific.
steps.companion_frame: Every life you build costs something. Be specific about what you traded away to get here: morning rides, deep friendships, the feeling of being in your body instead of trapped in your head. This isn't regret — it's inventory.
steps.probe: Past the obvious. What's the quiet one you don't usually let yourself miss?

steps.title: How far, honestly
steps.prompt: Honestly, how far are you from that version of you right now?
steps.companion_frame: On a normal week right now — how far are you from that buried version of you? A little dusty, or a stranger? There's no failing grade. The distance is just the starting line, and you can't close a gap you won't look at.
steps.probe: Don't soften it to feel better. The real distance is the one we get to close.

close.companion: That's your honest inventory — what it cost, and how far the drift ran. Not to sit in, to push off from. I've put it in your Playbook to keep or cut.
close.prompt: Ready to see what's on the other side?

assets.title: The Window
assets.summary: See the two Tuesdays — who you become if nothing changes, and if it does.
assets.produces: the spark — your ordinary Tuesday, reclaimed

steps.title: The window
steps.prompt: Picture the Tuesday a year out if nothing changes. What does it look like?
steps.companion_frame: There's a window between who you are today and who you keep saying you'll be. Most people never look through it. Today you look: picture an ordinary Tuesday a year from now if nothing changes. Sit with that profile for a second.
steps.probe: Not the disaster version — the ordinary one. How do you wake up, what do you reach for?

steps.title: The other window
steps.prompt: Now the Tuesday where you did the work — what's different by 7am?
steps.companion_frame: Now the other Tuesday — same year out, but you've been doing the work. What's different by 7am? Not the highlight reel. The ordinary stuff: how you wake up, what you reach for, how you move. That's the spark we're going to protect.
steps.probe: Make it ordinary and real — not the medal, the morning.

close.companion: That second Tuesday is the spark. Hold onto it — everything from here is about making it the real one. I've saved it to your Playbook to keep or cut.
close.prompt: Ready to turn it into something you can chase?

assets.title: Build Your Reclaim List
assets.summary: Turn the vision into specific, checkable things you want back.

steps.title: Build the Reclaim List
steps.prompt: List the specific things you want back — three to start.
steps.companion_frame: Turn that second Tuesday into real, specific things you want back. Riding before work without dreading it. Keeping up on the trail. Recognizing the person in the mirror. Give me a few — three to start, more if they keep coming. This becomes your Reclaim List.
steps.probe: Make them things you'd notice when they happen, not vague wishes. What's checkable?

steps.title: Make each one checkable
steps.prompt: Take one item and make it checkable — what would it look like in your week?
steps.companion_frame: Let's sharpen one. Say you want to 'feel like an athlete again' — what would the Athlete actually be doing on a Tuesday that you're not doing now? We do this for each item, so every goal is something we can both see when it happens.
steps.probe: If you couldn't tell whether you'd done it, sharpen it. What's the version you'd both see?

close.companion: That's your Reclaim List — the whole point, in your own words. It lives on your dashboard, and we'll check things off it together as you win them back.
close.prompt: Lock these onto your dashboard?

assets.title: The IDQ
assets.summary: The honest mirror — your starting read across four dimensions. Retakes every 60 days.

assets.title: Identity Excavation
assets.summary: Dig up the buried self and name who you're reclaiming.

steps.title: The archaeological dig
steps.prompt: What did you used to do that made you feel most like yourself?
steps.companion_frame: Start with the body memory — the thing you did that lit you up. Don't analyze it yet; just put us there. When were you most alive?
steps.probe: One real scene beats a category. When, where, who was around — put me in it.

steps.title: Your identity knows
steps.prompt: Who were you when you did it — not the activity, the person?
steps.companion_frame: You told me what you did. Now tell me who you were — the person, not the activity. What did the people around you call you? Who did you become the moment you started?
steps.probe: Take your time. One honest sentence beats a paragraph of hedging — and don't shrink it. If you were good, say you were good.

steps.title: Make yourself the protagonist
steps.prompt: Tell it as your story — you in the center, not off to the side.
steps.companion_frame: Now put yourself at the center of it. Not a supporting role in someone else's life — the protagonist of your own. Say it like it's yours.
steps.probe: Where are you hedging yourself out of the lead? Take the credit that’s actually yours.

steps.title: Name the Reclaimed Identity
steps.prompt: Give that self a name to wear again.
steps.companion_frame: Name it — one phrase you can put on, like a title you wear. Natural case: “the Elite Cyclist”, “the Builder”. The self you’re reclaiming.
steps.probe: Make it yours — self-chosen, not a role someone else assigned you. What’s the version underneath?

assets.title: The Reconnect Checkpoint
assets.summary: The reconnection milestone — have you found yourself? Firm gate; opens Rewire.

assets.title: The Disinformation Audit
assets.summary: Catch the comfortable lies your mind runs to keep you safe and small — and take them apart.
assets.produces: the member's true line (in their words)

steps.title: The comfortable lie
steps.prompt: Write the lie you tell yourself most — in its own words, the way your head actually says it.
steps.companion_frame: Your mind runs a quiet campaign to keep you comfortable — and comfortable, right now, means stuck. It tells you things that sound like facts: 'too late for me,' 'I don't have the time,' 'this is just what fifty looks like.' Let's catch the loudest one.
steps.probe: That's the cleaned-up version. What does it sound like at 6am when the alarm goes off? Say it rawer.

steps.title: Cross-examine it
steps.prompt: Two honest columns: what's the real evidence this is true? And what's the evidence it's not?
steps.companion_frame: Now we put it on trial. A lie survives because no one ever asks it for evidence. What's the actual proof for it — and against it? 'Too old' is a story; the people who started at your age and didn't stop are the counter-evidence.
steps.probe: You found a lot against it and not much for it. So why have you been treating it like a verdict?

steps.title: Write the true line
steps.prompt: Write your true line. One sentence. True enough that you'd say it out loud.
steps.companion_frame: A lie you've disproven still needs something to stand in its place. Not a slogan — something true you can stand behind on a bad day. Mine was 'I'm out of shape, and I'm starting anyway.' Both halves true.
steps.probe: If it sounds like a motivational poster, it won't hold — make it sound like you.

close.companion: That's the audit. The lie won't vanish — but now you've got a line to answer it with. I've put your true line in your Playbook to keep or cut.
close.prompt: Next time the old line shows up, will you answer it with this one?

assets.title: The Numbers Exercise
assets.summary: Pull your real numbers and look at them without flinching — a baseline, not a verdict.

steps.title: Know your numbers
steps.prompt: Gather your numbers and put them down — whatever you can get today.
steps.companion_frame: Real change starts with the truth, and the truth here is numbers — not how you feel, not a guess. Pull what you can: weight, resting heart rate, blood pressure. We're not here to judge them. We're here to face them.
steps.probe: If one made you wince, that's the one that matters most. Don't round it kinder than it is.

steps.title: Look without flinching
steps.prompt: Write one sentence you want to remember about this starting line.
steps.companion_frame: Now look at them straight, without the flinch and without the story. This isn't your verdict — it's your starting line, and every starting line is a place to push off from.
steps.probe: Make it the version that steadies you, not the one that shames you.

close.companion: These are your baseline now — not a grade, a starting line. I've dropped your note into your Playbook to keep or cut.
close.prompt: Want me to track any of these so you can see them change?

assets.title: The Food Relationship Assessment
assets.summary: See what food is really doing for you — then try one new lens.

steps.title: Fuel, not comfort
steps.prompt: When you eat when you're not hungry — what's it really for?
steps.companion_frame: Quick honesty, no shame. When you eat and you're not hungry, what's it actually doing for you — comfort, reward, boredom? Naming food's real job is the first move toward changing it.
steps.probe: Go past 'stress.' What's the feeling right before you reach for it?

steps.title: One reframe
steps.prompt: Write your food reframe — 'Food is ___ for the ___ I'm reclaiming.'
steps.companion_frame: Try this lens for one meal today: food as fuel for the person you're reclaiming — not a reward you earned, not a punishment. A new relationship with food gets built one plate at a time.
steps.probe: Name the actual identity — 'for the cyclist,' 'for the dad who keeps up.'

close.companion: That's a new deal with food — a lens you can carry. I've put your reframe in your Playbook to keep or cut.
close.prompt: Use this lens at your next meal?

assets.title: The Visualization Workshop
assets.summary: Use the trick athletes use — rehearse the hard thing before it happens.

steps.title: Why this isn't woo
steps.prompt: Pick the moment you most want to handle better — the 6am alarm, the hill, the room you walk into. Name it.
steps.companion_frame: Athletes picture the shot before they take it because the brain barely tells a vividly imagined action from a real one — same pathways fire. It's a skill, not a vibe, and you can build it.
steps.probe: Make it specific and real — a moment you'll meet this week, not a someday.

steps.title: Rehearse the feeling
steps.prompt: Run it, then write what it felt like to get through it.
steps.companion_frame: Run the tape for sixty seconds. Don't picture the outcome — feel it. The effort, the breath, standing a little taller after. That rehearsal is what you draw on when the real moment comes.
steps.probe: You described what happened. What did it feel like in your body when you didn't quit?

close.companion: You just practiced winning before it happened. I've saved what it felt like to your Playbook to keep or cut.
close.prompt: Run this once more before the moment this week?

assets.title: The Self-Talk Audit
assets.summary: Catch how you talk to yourself, and rewrite one line true-but-forgiving.

steps.title: Catch the voice
steps.prompt: Write the harshest thing you say to yourself when you mess up — word for word.
steps.companion_frame: For a day, listen to how you talk to yourself when you slip. Would you say it to a friend you respect? Most of us run an inner coach we'd fire on the spot. You can't change a voice you haven't heard.
steps.probe: That's the printable version. What's the actual word you use? Write the real one.

steps.title: Reframe one line
steps.prompt: Rewrite your line — true, but on your side.
steps.companion_frame: Take that harsh line and rewrite it true but forgiving. 'I always quit' becomes 'I've stopped before, and I'm here again.' Forgiving yourself isn't going soft — it's how the change survives a bad day.
steps.probe: If it sounds fake-positive, you won't believe it. Keep the truth in it.

close.companion: You just fired the coach you'd never have hired. I've put your reframed line in your Playbook to keep or cut.
close.prompt: Catch yourself once this week and use the new line?

assets.title: The False Start Protocol
assets.summary: Decide your clip-back-in move now, while it's calm — before the slip.

steps.title: Setbacks are built in
steps.prompt: Be honest — what does your slip usually look like? How does a good run fall apart?
steps.companion_frame: Setbacks are part of the process, not proof you failed. The people who make it aren't the ones who never slip — they're the ones who don't let a slip become a slide. Let's build your plan for the slip before it happens.
steps.probe: Name the real pattern, not the excuse. What's the first domino?

steps.title: Your clip-back-in move
steps.prompt: Write your clip-back-in move — the one tiny thing that means you're back.
steps.companion_frame: Write your return move while it's calm: the smallest action that counts as clipping back in after a missed day. Not a redemption arc — one rep. Decide it now, so the next-day you doesn't have to negotiate.
steps.probe: Smaller. Make it so easy you can't talk yourself out of it on the worst day.

close.companion: Now the slip has a plan, and a plan beats willpower. I've put your move in your Playbook to keep or cut.
close.prompt: If you miss this week, will you run this move?

assets.title: The Rewire Checkpoint
assets.summary: Has the frame moved? Opens the deeper Rebuild work.

assets.title: The First Step Assessment
assets.summary: Pick the movement you'll actually do, and set an honest starting line.

steps.title: Pick the vehicle
steps.prompt: What's your vehicle — the movement you'll actually come back to?
steps.companion_frame: Time to move — but the best exercise isn't the 'optimal' one, it's the one you'll actually do on a cold Wednesday. Walking is the most popular for a reason; cycling's right behind it.
steps.probe: Be honest about your real life, not your ideal one. What fits the week you actually have?

steps.title: Where you're starting
steps.prompt: How far or how long can you go today before it gets hard?
steps.companion_frame: An honest baseline — how long can you go before it gets hard? No target, no judgment. We build from where you actually are, because that's the only place a foundation holds.
steps.probe: Don't inflate it. The real number is the one we can build on.

close.companion: That's your vehicle and your starting line. I've put your starting line in your Playbook to keep or cut.
close.prompt: Want me to track this so you can watch it climb?

assets.title: The Invisible Foundations
assets.summary: Shore up one of the unseen basics that hold everything together.
assets.produces: your foundation pick for the week

steps.title: The stuff nobody sees
steps.prompt: Pick one invisible foundation to shore up this week — water, mobility, or breaking up sitting.
steps.companion_frame: The work that actually holds is invisible: hydration, a little mobility, not sitting for nine hours. Cutting your sedentary hours buys you benefits beyond your workout minutes.
steps.probe: Which one, honestly, are you worst at? Start there.

close.companion: Small and invisible, but it's the base the visible stuff stands on. I've put your pick in your Playbook to keep or cut.
close.prompt: Make this a daily clip-in?

assets.title: Sleep & Recover
assets.summary: Treat recovery as part of the work — and pull one lever to sleep better.

steps.title: Recovery is the work
steps.prompt: Honestly — how's your sleep right now?
steps.companion_frame: You don't get stronger during the effort — you get stronger during the recovery, when the body rebuilds. Skip it and you keep almost none of the gains.
steps.probe: Past 'fine.' How many real hours, and how often do you wake up?

steps.title: Pick one lever
steps.prompt: Pick your one sleep lever for this week.
steps.companion_frame: We don't fix sleep all at once — we pull one lever. A fixed wind-down, screens off earlier, a darker room. Just one. The one you'll actually do tonight.
steps.probe: Make it the easy one you'll actually do tonight.

close.companion: Recovery isn't time off from the work — it is the work. I've saved your sleep lever to your Playbook to keep or cut.
close.prompt: Run this lever every night this week?

assets.title: The Fuel Plan
assets.summary: Build a way of eating you have, not one you go on.

steps.title: A diet you have
steps.prompt: What's one swap you'd actually keep — for good, not for a month?
steps.companion_frame: A diet isn't something you go on and white-knuckle until you fail — it's something you have. More real food, less added sugar and ultra-processed stuff. Not perfect. Sustainable.
steps.probe: If it sounds like a punishment, you won't keep it. What's a swap you'd barely miss?

steps.title: The thermostat
steps.prompt: Write the one line that keeps you off the crash-diet cycle.
steps.companion_frame: Keeping weight off means moving your set point — slowly, like a thermostat. Crash diets fight it and lose. We move it instead, and it stays moved.
steps.probe: Make it yours — the line you'll remember at week three when the scale stalls.

close.companion: That's a way of eating you can actually keep. I've put your swap and your line in your Playbook to keep or cut.
close.prompt: Start with this swap this week?

assets.title: The Movement Menu
assets.summary: Build your real week of movement around the floor, not the ceiling.
assets.produces: your weekly movement plan (and a daily dose clip-in)

steps.title: Build the week
steps.prompt: Lay out your week — what days, what times does the movement happen?
steps.companion_frame: Aim for the floor first: about 150 minutes of moderate movement — roughly thirty minutes, five days. That's the floor that changes your health. Lock the floor before you chase the ceiling.
steps.probe: Put it on real days at real times. When this week, specifically?

close.companion: That's your week, on real days. I've put it in your Playbook to keep or cut.
close.prompt: Turn on the daily movement check-in?

assets.title: The Rebuild Checkpoint
assets.summary: The numbers begin to move — pull them against your baseline.

assets.title: Reclaim Readiness
assets.summary: Notice the reclaimed you starting to show up — and choose what to build next.

steps.title: Are you carrying it yet
steps.prompt: Where have you caught a glimpse of the reclaimed you lately — even for a second?
steps.companion_frame: Reclaim isn't a finish line — it's the moment the person you've been rebuilding starts showing up in the wider world. Are you starting to feel like the person on your list — even a little?
steps.probe: Don't wait for the dramatic version. When did you last surprise yourself?

steps.title: Agency, not arrival
steps.prompt: Which of the three do you most want to build next?
steps.companion_frame: Reclaiming means you've got the wheel. Aging well comes down to meaningful activity, close relationships, and a sense of purpose. Reclaim goes after all three, deliberately.
steps.probe: Pick the one that's been quietest lately. That's usually the one calling.

close.companion: You're not arriving — you're taking the wheel. I've put your direction in your Playbook to keep or cut.
close.prompt: Build toward that next?

assets.title: Your Success Story
assets.summary: Say the story of one thing you got back, in your own words.
assets.produces: your success story (seed for the Legacy Letter)

steps.title: Say it in your words
steps.prompt: Tell the story of one thing you reclaimed — and what it felt like to notice it.
steps.companion_frame: Tell me the story of one thing you got back — out loud, in your own words. Not the metrics. What it felt like the first time you noticed the old you was back in the room.
steps.probe: You gave me the what. Give me the moment — where were you when you felt it?

close.companion: That's your story now, in your own words. I've saved it to your Playbook to keep or cut.
close.prompt: Keep this one close?

assets.title: Adventure Planning
assets.summary: Put a measuring-stick event on the calendar, and back-plan the build.
assets.produces: your measuring-stick event (to the Reclaim List)

steps.title: Put a measuring stick on the calendar
steps.prompt: Name a real event or trip — with a date — that scares and excites you.
steps.companion_frame: A reclaimed identity needs a proving ground — something real on the calendar that scares and excites you. The thing that lets you say 'I did this.' when it's done. Half the joy is the build-up.
steps.probe: Put a date on it. A someday isn't a measuring stick — when?

steps.title: Back-plan the build
steps.prompt: Work backward — what does the first build week look like?
steps.companion_frame: Work backward from the date. What does your body need to handle that day, and what's the base you build in the quiet weeks before? You prepare so the day is a celebration, not a survival.
steps.probe: Start with this week. What's the very first session toward it?

close.companion: Now it's real — a date, and a path to it. I've added the event to your Reclaim List and put the plan in your Playbook to keep or cut.
close.prompt: Add the event to your Reclaim List?

assets.title: Bigger World Audit
assets.summary: Find where your world went small, and push one edge back out.
assets.produces: the edge you'll push out this month

steps.title: Widen the circle
steps.prompt: Where has your world gone small — and what's one edge you'd push back out this month?
steps.companion_frame: The Fade shrinks your world — the places you stopped going, the things you stopped saying yes to. Reclaim widens it back. Where has your world gone small? Then we pick one edge to push back out.
steps.probe: Not the easy one. What's the yes that scares you a little?

close.companion: That's the circle widening again — on purpose, by your hand. I've put your edge in your Playbook to keep or cut.
close.prompt: Go after that edge this month?

assets.title: Invitation Exercise
assets.summary: Bring someone with you — and find the words that actually land.

steps.title: Come do this with me
steps.prompt: Who would you invite to do this with you?
steps.companion_frame: Here's how this stops being a solo act: you bring someone. The door opens through relationships, not credentials. Who would you say 'come do this with me' to? Not to coach them — just to share the thing that gave you yourself back.
steps.probe: Picture their face. Who came to mind first? Trust that.

steps.title: The words that matter
steps.prompt: Write the message you'd actually send them.
steps.companion_frame: The line that lands isn't 'you should exercise more.' It's 'I know what you're capable of.' That's the line that got said to me. That's the line I said to Gary.
steps.probe: Lead with belief in them, not advice. What would make them feel seen?

close.companion: That's how the comeback spreads — one person, one real message. I've put it in your Playbook to keep or cut.
close.prompt: Send it this week?

assets.title: Social Connection
assets.summary: Find the place you actually belong — not just attend.

steps.title: Find your people
steps.prompt: Where's one place you could really belong — and show up for real?
steps.companion_frame: Belonging beats attending. Social support is one of the strongest predictors of change that sticks — and a real buffer against stress. Where do you belong, or want to? Not where you show up — where you're missed when you don't.
steps.probe: Belonging, not attending. Where would they notice if you were gone?

close.companion: That's the difference between attending and belonging — and belonging holds the whole thing up. I've put your place in your Playbook to keep or cut.
close.prompt: Show up there this month?

assets.title: Legacy Letter
assets.summary: Write it forward — and name the Loop.

steps.title: Write it forward
steps.prompt: Write your letter — short is fine. What do you want them to know is still possible?
steps.companion_frame: Write a short letter to someone who'll read it later — a kid, a friend, the next person walking through the door you came through. What did you reclaim, and what do you want them to know is still possible in midlife?
steps.probe: Write it to one real person, not 'whoever.' Who needs to hear this from you?

steps.title: The Loop, named
steps.prompt: What's the next thing the Loop is already calling you toward?
steps.companion_frame: The finish line moves. You'll reclaim these things, life will shift, the list will re-form, and you'll go again. That's not failure — that's the design. It's why it's Grinta for Life.
steps.probe: You're not done — you're between laps. What's pulling at you next?

close.companion: That's a letter forward and a name for what comes next. The work doesn't end — it loops, and you're stronger at the start of each one. This one, I'd keep.
close.prompt: Ready to name the next lap?

doors.descriptor: The role that ended, plateaued, or a retirement that became a freefall.
The role reversal that made you the one doing the caring.
The house that got quiet when the kids left.
The friendships that slipped away without a goodbye.
The body that started saying no to what it used to do easily.
The mirror moment you couldn’t look away from.
The drift from partnership into just coexisting.
Losing someone close, and everything changing after.
The house filling up — marriage, young kids, everyone needing you — and no space left for yourself.

physical: Your body feels like it belongs to you — you know it, you trust it, you’re at home in it.
If you wanted to ask something real of your body today — something demanding — you could, without bracing for it to hurt.
You know your numbers — weight, blood pressure, resting heart rate — and you can look at them without looking away.
You’re as physically capable today as you were five years ago.
The way you eat is something you actually decide — not something running on autopilot.
You sleep well, and you wake up with the day in front of you as something to show up for.
self: If your twenty-five-year-old self walked in right now, they’d recognize the person you’ve become.
You regularly make time for things you care about that have nothing to do with work or anyone else’s needs.
Asked “who are you?”, you’ve got an answer that isn’t your job title or your role in the family.
You haven’t quietly traded away something you loved to make room for something you don’t.
The life you’re in right now is one you chose, on purpose — eyes open.
You’re the main character in your own story, not the supporting cast in everyone else’s.
social: There’s at least one person in your life who sees the real you and tells you the truth.
You show up all the way for the people you love — actually present, not just in the room.
You’re the one who calls, who plans, who says yes — the one who shows up, not the one who bails.
Your closest relationships have gotten deeper this past year, not thinner.
You belong somewhere — a group, a community — really belong, not just attend.
When someone asks how you’re doing, you tell them the truth.
outlook: You’ve got a clear picture of what you want your next chapter to be, past what you’re obligated to do.
In the last six months you’ve set a goal that genuinely excites you — yours, not one handed to you.
You’re willing to do hard things on purpose, because of who they’re turning you into.
Picture the next ten years — you can see specific moments you want to be inside of.
In the last month you did something because the person you’re becoming would do it.
You believe your best chapters are still ahead — and you’re willing to bet on it.

reflections.text: There's a moment most days when you feel most like a stranger to yourself. Noticing exactly when it hits — that isn't weakness. It's the start of the way back.

The Fade: the slow drift away from the person you used to be — built not from one disaster but from a hundred reasonable decisions. Naming it doesn't fix it. It means you stop pretending it isn't there.
This was never about a program that tells you what to eat and checks whether you obeyed. It's the opposite — you run your own comeback. The tools are in your hands, and you're not doing it alone.
An honest read of where you're starting doesn't need studying for, and there's no score to pass. A few of the answers will sting. That sting is the point — it's the gap, finally in view.

How far you've drifted comes down to four things: your body, your sense of self, the people around you, and where you're headed. It's a slow, honest measure — real change in who you are doesn't jump week to week.
Real change in who you are doesn't move week to week — it moves over seasons. When you measure again, let it be still if it's still. Slow and real beats fast and fake.

The gap rarely opens all at once. For most people it traces to a single door — a career cliff, an aging parent, an empty nest, a diagnosis, a loss. Knowing which one is yours is the start of walking back through it.
Most people walked through more than one door. There's no prize for keeping your story simple — the truth is what lets you be met where you actually are.
The door you came through is one a lot of good people have walked through — and most never had a name for it. Naming it doesn't fix it. It means you stop pretending it isn't there.

What did twelve-year-old you do when nobody was watching — the thing you lost track of time in, before mortgages and meetings? The sport, the instrument, the thing you quit because it 'wasn't practical.' That's probably your vein of gold.
Your mind will lie to you — too old, too far gone, too busy. Your identity knows better. It isn't gone; it's buried under decades of being responsible. Who were you, underneath all the roles?

You've spent years as a supporting character in everyone else's story — the company's, the kids', the partner's. All worthy. None of them yours. You deserve a story that's yours too. That isn't selfish. It's overdue.
Put a word on the person you're bringing back — the Athlete, the Builder, the Friend. It doesn't have to be perfect. It has to be true enough to aim at.
Every life you build costs something — the morning rides, the deep friendships, the feeling of being in your body instead of trapped in your head. Naming what you traded isn't regret. It's inventory.
The distance between you and the buried version of you isn't a failing grade. It's a starting line. And you can't close a gap you won't look at.
There's a window between who you are today and who you keep saying you'll be. Picture an ordinary Tuesday a year from now if nothing changes. Most people never look. Looking is the first brave thing.
Now the other Tuesday — a year out, but you've done the work. Not the highlight reel; the ordinary stuff. How you wake up, what you reach for, how you move. That's the spark worth protecting.

The future you want isn't a feeling — it's specific. Riding before work without dreading it. Keeping up on the trail. Recognizing the person in the mirror. The clearer you name what you want back, the more real it becomes.
'Feel like an athlete again' stays a wish until you ask: what would the Athlete actually be doing on a Tuesday that you're not doing now? A goal you can picture is a goal you can reach.
Your mind runs a quiet campaign to keep you comfortable: 'too late for me,' 'I don't have time,' 'this is just what fifty looks like.' Naming the loudest lie is how you stop obeying it.
Take the lie to court. 'Too old' is a story; the people who started at your age and didn't stop are the counter-evidence. Most of these don't survive being looked at directly.

Replace the lie with one true sentence you can stand behind — not a slogan, something you believe. 'I'm out of shape and I'm starting anyway.' That's the line you come back to when the old one gets loud.
Real change starts with an honest look at where you actually are — not a guess, not how you feel. Facing the numbers isn't judgment. It's information you can finally use.
A baseline you can see without looking away is a starting line, not a verdict. That clarity is what makes it possible to set goals that mean something.

Athletes picture the shot before they take it because the brain barely tells a vividly imagined action from a real one — the same pathways fire. Rehearsing the hard thing is a skill, and you can build it.

Run the tape for sixty seconds: finishing a hard effort, the confidence after, standing a little taller. Don't picture the outcome — feel it. That rehearsal is what you draw on when the real moment comes.
When you eat off-plan, notice what it's really doing for you — hunger, or comfort, reward, boredom. No shame in the answer. Naming food's real job is the first move toward changing it.
Try one lens today: food as fuel for the person you're reclaiming — not a reward, not a punishment. A new relationship with food gets built one plate at a time.
Setbacks are part of the process, not proof you failed. The people who make it aren't the ones who never slip — they're the ones who don't let a slip become a slide.
Decide your return move while it's calm: the smallest action that counts as clipping back in after a missed day. Not a redemption arc — one rep. Decide it now so the next-day you doesn't have to.
Notice how you talk to yourself when you mess up. Would you say it to a friend you respect? Most of us run a coach we'd never tolerate from anyone else. Hearing it is step one.
Take one harsh line and rewrite it true but forgiving. 'I always quit' becomes 'I've stopped before, and I'm here again.' Forgiving yourself isn't going soft — it's how the change survives a bad day.
Ask honestly: has anything shifted in how you think about your body, your food, or what's possible? Even one belief looser than it was is the ground the next stretch of work stands on.
You don't have to be 'done' thinking to start moving. You only have to have shifted the frame enough that the building will hold. That's what readiness actually is.
The best exercise is the one you'll actually do. Walking's the most popular for a reason; cycling's right behind it. Pick the thing you won't talk yourself out of by Wednesday.
An honest baseline — how long you can go before it gets hard — isn't a judgment. It's the only place a foundation holds: where you actually are.
Some days the whole job is seven minutes. Nobody white-knuckles a full workout from a dead start — but anyone can do seven, and seven is usually enough to remember why you started.
The deal: you only owe seven minutes. Stop after with a clean conscience if you want. Most days you won't want to — that's not willpower, it's momentum, and it's on your side now.
The work nobody sees is the work that holds: water, a little mobility, not sitting for nine hours straight. Shoring up one invisible foundation buys you more than the workout alone.

A diet isn't something you go on — it's something you have. The pattern that lasts is the one you can sustain: more real food, less of the processed stuff. One swap you'd actually keep beats ten you won't.
Keeping weight off isn't about crash dieting — it's about nudging your set point, slowly, like a thermostat. Crash diets fight the thermostat and lose. The slow move is the one that holds.
Aim for the floor first: about 150 minutes of moderate movement a week — roughly thirty minutes, five days. Lock the floor before you chase the ceiling.
A 'yes' feeds the streak. A 'no' after a run of yeses is just life — and the next yes is the one that counts most.
Gary rode 1,052 miles his first year at 250-plus pounds, on flat roads and a trainer. The number was never the point — the consistency it forced was. Pick a total that scares you a little.
The base gets built in the cold months, on the trainer, when nobody's watching. That's the part that makes the big day possible. Every small unit is a vote for who you're becoming.
You don't get stronger during the effort — you get stronger during the recovery, when the body rebuilds. Sleep isn't time off from the work. It's part of it.
Set today's numbers next to where you started. Something's usually moving — capacity, weight, how the stairs feel. That's the measuring stick doing its job.

Reclaim isn't a finish line — it's the moment the recovered you starts showing up in the wider world. Are you beginning to feel like the person on your list, even a little? No rush. The Loop comes back around either way.

Reclaiming doesn't mean you were broken. It means you've got the agency to direct what comes next — on purpose. Aging well comes down to three things: meaningful activity, close relationships, and a sense of purpose.

Tell the story of one thing you got back — not the metrics, but what it felt like the first time you noticed the old you was back in the room. Saying it out loud makes it real, and easier to defend when doubt returns.
A reclaimed identity needs a proving ground. Pick a real event that scares and excites you — the one that lets you say 'I did this' when it's done. Half the joy is the build-up.
You don't fight conditions on the big day — you prepare in the quiet weeks so the day is a celebration, not a survival. Work backward from the date.
The Fade shrinks your world; Reclaim widens it back. Where has yours gone small — the places you stopped going, the things you stopped saying yes to? Push one edge back out.

The door opens through relationships, not credentials. Who would you say 'come do this with me' to? Reaching out to one person — not to coach them, just to share it — is how this becomes a movement instead of a solo act.
The line that lands isn't 'you should exercise more.' It's 'I know what you're capable of.' Who in your life needs to hear it from you?
Belonging beats attending. Social support is one of the strongest predictors of change that sticks — and a real buffer against stress. Where's one place you could really show up?
Imagine writing to someone who'll read it later — a kid, a friend, the next person walking through your door. What did you reclaim, and what do you want them to know is still possible in midlife?

The finish line moves. You'll reclaim these, life will shift, and the list will re-form. That's not failure — it's the design. It's why it's Grinta for Life. When you're ready, you clip back in and go again.
Some days the whole job is just to clip in. Not perfect. In.
Plenty is out of your hands today. Name one thing that isn't — and do that. Control is a muscle.
Pick one thing today that's a little harder than it needs to be — on purpose, because of who it's turning you into.
Missed yesterday? Then today's the rep that matters most. The slip isn't the story; the return is. Clip back in.
Keep the reason you started somewhere you'll see it. Motivation fades; a reason you can read doesn't.
There's always a moment everyone's struggling — and the one with more Grinta keeps going. That's not a feeling. It's a decision. Make it once today.
One off day is a slip. Three is a slide. You're allowed the slip — just don't let today be day two.
Reach out to one person in your corner — a check-in, a plan, a 'come do this with me.' Connection is fuel, and it runs both ways.
Is there a stretch effort on your horizon? Without one, the work goes flat. Put one small challenge on the calendar.
If you're running the harsh tape about yourself, cut it. Forgiveness isn't softness — it's how the change survives. One kind, true line, then go.
Don't chase the streak for its own sake. Chase the person it's building. If the streak breaks, the person doesn't.
Picture the Tuesday a year out if you keep going. Then go do one small thing your future self would thank you for.
